newsitem.title: INDIA: Indian soymeal exports to dip, China major buyer.
newsitem.headline: Indian soymeal exports to dip, China major buyer.

text.p: China has emerged as a major buyer of Indian soymeal in a growing world market but exports this year are expected to dip due to tight domestic supplies, officials and traders said on Tuesday.

"The market looks very healthy and demand is encouraging but sellers are a bit cautious in making heavy commitments," said Davish Jain, chairman of the Soybean Processors' Association of India (SOPA), based in the central Indian city of Indore.
"This year the star buyer is China," Jain told Reuters by telephone. "We think they will buy about half a million tonnes this year."
Tarun Kumar of Space Group, a leading Delhi exporter, said the Chinese buyers this year were making a spate of inquiries.
"Within a week's time I see more business coming from China," Kumar said.
Jain said export availability of soymeal this year would be lower because of a projected dip in soybean output in 1996/97 (November-October).
SOPA has estimated the 1996/97 output at 4.0 million tonnes against last year's 4.45 million. But traders expect the output to be lower than SOPA's estimates.
"We are expecting a crop of around 3.5 million tonnes," said S.N. Saboo of S.S. Mercantile, a leading oilmeal broker.

"Delay in the onset of monsoon, intermittent heavy downpour, continued cloudy weather, lack of dry spells with bright sunshine and finally heavy rains in the third and fourth week of October all contributed to the fall in the output," Saboo said.
Jain said India has committed more than 1.0 million tonnes of soymeal for export from the 1996/97 crop, compared to 1.5 million at this time last year.
He said the industry expected about two million tonnes of soymeal exports in 1996/97, sharply lower than 2.5 million in the previous year, due to a production shortfall.
He said this year China had already bought more than 300,000 tonnes of soymeal, the quantity it purchased during the whole of the 1995/96 season.
Indonesia, with purchases of 400,000 tonnes, was the largest buyer of Indian soymeal in 1995/96.
Besides Indonesia and China, Indian soymeal is in demand in Malaysia, Philippines, United Arab Emirates and South Korea.
The United States, Argentina and Brazil are the world's largest soymeal exporters. Brazil and Argentina have already sold their stocks and are not aggressive players in global markets.

Kumar said a welcome new trend this year was that Chinese firms, both private and state-owned, were contacting Indian companies directly. Earlier, China used to buy through Hong Kong based trading companies, he said.
Kumar said China preferred Indian soymeal because it could import smaller consignments of 10,000-12,000 tonnes, compared to U.S. supplies which come in huge consignments.
Traders said Indian soymeal was currently quoted at $278-279 per tonne F.A.S (free alongside ship) compared to $215 at the same time last year.
Soybean arrivals in the markets of central India were currently around 20,000 tonnes, the same as last year.
Jain said there was an annual domestic demand of about 600,000 tonnes, mainly for poultry feed.
He said there was no dearth of markets for Indian soymeal and it needed to increase soybean productivity and expand crop area to meet growing overseas demand.
